title: Calculate an 18% tip
concept: 18% is one of the most common tip amounts — but it's awkward because it's not a round number. The trick is to never try to calculate 18% in one step.
shortcut: Find 10% by moving the decimal one place left. Take half of that for 5%. Add a small 3% bump (roughly 30 cents per $10). Or skip the math entirely: double the tax line on your receipt — in most US states that's close to 18%.

title: The 10% trick
concept: 10% is the foundation of all tip math. Moving the decimal one place left gives you 10% of any number instantly. From there you can build any tip in seconds.
shortcut: 10% of $65 = $6.50 (just move the decimal). Double it for 20% = $13.00. Add half for 15% = $9.75. Master this one move and every tip becomes a two-second calculation.

title: 20% in one step
concept: 20% is exactly twice 10%. Since you already know how to find 10% instantly by moving the decimal left, you can always nail a 20% tip in two steps — no guessing, no fumbling with the calculator at the table.
shortcut: Move the decimal left (10%), then double it (20%). Bill $65 → 10% = $6.50 → double → $13.00 tip, $78.00 total. 20% is both the easiest tip to calculate precisely and the standard expectation at most restaurants in the US.

title: Tip on subtotal or total?
concept: In the US, tipping on the pre-tax subtotal is technically correct — you're tipping on the service, not the government's cut. Many people tip on the full total because it's easier. The difference is small but adds up on larger bills.
shortcut: Pre-tax tip is always the lower number. On a $50 meal with 10% tax, 20% pre-tax = $10 vs 20% post-tax = $11. Both are acceptable — knowing the difference means you're making a deliberate choice, not leaving money on the table by accident.

title: Split the bill right
concept: Always add the tip to the full bill before splitting. If you split first then tip separately, each person tips on a smaller amount and the server gets shortchanged.
shortcut: The right order: Total → add tip → divide by people. A $80 bill with 20% tip becomes $96 total. Split 4 ways: $24 each. Never divide first — you lose cents in rounding and everyone underpays.

title: The 25% shortcut
concept: 25% off means you pay 75% of the original price. Since 25% equals one quarter (¼), you can find the discount instantly by dividing the price by 4.
shortcut: Divide by 4 to find 25% of any price. That's your savings. Subtract from original to get the sale price. For 50% off, divide by 2. For 10% off, just move the decimal.

title: 10% off — the gateway discount
concept: 10% is the foundation of all discount math. It's the easiest percentage to calculate: just move the decimal point one place to the left. Every other discount — 20%, 25%, 30% — is built from this single move.
shortcut: Move the decimal left to find 10%. $80 → $8 off. $120 → $12 off. For 20% off, double that number. For 5% off, halve it. This one move unlocks every discount on any price tag.

title: Buy 2 get 1 free — the real math
concept: "Buy 2 get 1 free" is 33% off, not 50%. You pay for 2 items and receive 3. The free item's cost is spread across all three, so each item effectively costs two-thirds of the full price.
shortcut: Per-item cost = (2 × full price) ÷ 3. Total saving = 1 full item's price. For $9 shampoo: pay $18 for 3 → $6 per bottle, save $9 total. Ask: do you actually need all 3?
example:
Shampoo: $9.00 each
Buy 2 get 1 free
You pay: $18.00 for 3
Per bottle = $6.00
Total saving = $9.00

title: Stacking discounts
concept: Two discounts stacked together don't simply add up. 20% off plus 10% off is NOT 30% off — the second discount applies to the already-reduced price. You always save a little less than the sum suggests.
shortcut: Apply discounts one at a time. $100 → 20% off → $80 → 10% off $80 → $72. Saving: $28, not $30. Quick rule: each 10% combo loses about 1% to stacking. Two 50%-off coupons would only be 75% off, not 100%.

title: Compare unit prices
concept: Bigger packs look cheaper, but they're not always cheaper per item. Divide the total price by the number of items to find the unit price — the true cost of one — so you can make a fair comparison.
shortcut: Unit price = total price ÷ quantity. 6-pack for $7.20 → $7.20 ÷ 6 = $1.20 each. Singles at $1.49? The pack wins. Always check before you grab the bigger size — it's not always the better deal.
example:
6-pack: $7.20
÷ 6 items = $1.20 each
Singles: $1.49 each
Pack saves: $0.29 per item

title: Is this within my budget?
concept: Knowing if you can afford something isn't just about the price tag — it's about what you have left after everything else. Subtract your known expenses from your total budget and compare the remainder to what you're considering buying.
shortcut: Budget − what you've spent = what's left. If the item costs less than what's left, you're fine. Build this as a 10-second mental check before any discretionary purchase: what's my budget, what have I spent, what's remaining?
example:
Budget: $150.00
Groceries: $45.00
Transport: $20.00
Remaining: $85.00
Item costs $79.99 → within budget ✓

title: Monthly ↔ yearly costs
concept: Subscription services quote monthly prices because they look smaller. $12.99/month sounds cheap until you realise it's $155.88/year. Always convert to yearly before subscribing — it's the only way to see the real annual impact on your budget.
shortcut: Monthly → yearly: multiply by 12. Yearly → monthly: divide by 12. $10/month = $120/year. $99/year = $8.25/month. When comparing plans, always put them on the same basis — monthly vs monthly, or yearly vs yearly.

title: Price per use
concept: The real cost of anything isn't the sticker price — it's the cost per use. A $30 item used 100 times costs $0.30 per use. The same $30 item used only 5 times costs $6.00 per use. Thinking in cost-per-use reveals which purchases actually have value.
shortcut: Cost per use = total price ÷ estimated uses. A $100 gym membership for 50 sessions = $2 per session. A $5 coffee machine pod = $5 per cup. Estimate your realistic usage honestly — that's the number that matters.
example:
Coffee maker: $60.00
Uses per year: 300
Cost per cup: $0.20
Café coffee: $4.50/cup
Annual saving: $1,290

title: Add sales tax in your head
concept: Sales tax is usually 6–10% depending on your state. Since it's close to 10%, use 10% as your anchor and nudge down. You'll be within cents every time.
shortcut: For 8% tax: find 10% (move the decimal left), then subtract 20% of that. On a $40 item: 10% = $4.00, minus $0.80 = $3.20 tax. Total = $43.20. Rounding up to 10% and ignoring the rest works fine for budgeting.

title: Estimate your cart total
concept: You don't need exact prices to stay on budget. Round each item to the nearest dollar as you shop, keep a running mental sum, and you'll hit the register knowing you're covered.
shortcut: Round every item up: $3.79 → $4, $8.49 → $9, $1.19 → $2. Add the rounded numbers. Your estimate will land a dollar or two above the actual total — exactly the right direction for budgeting. Never try to track cents.

title: Gross vs net — what you actually keep
concept: Your gross pay is what you earn before taxes. Net pay is what arrives in your bank account. Between federal tax, state tax, Social Security, and Medicare, most workers keep 70–75 cents of every dollar earned. Always plan your budget with net, never gross.
shortcut: Quick estimate: take 25–30% off gross to get net. Earning $3,000/month gross? Expect $2,100–$2,250 net. For annual salary: divide by 12 to get monthly gross, then knock off 25–30% for a working budget number.
example:
Gross pay: $3,000/month
−25% deductions = $750
Net pay ≈ $2,250

$60,000 salary
÷ 12 = $5,000/month gross
−25% = $3,750 net

title: What a % raise really adds
concept: A percentage raise sounds exciting, but the real number is what lands in your paycheck. A 5% raise on $60,000 is $3,000 more per year — about $250/month before taxes. Knowing the actual dollar impact helps you negotiate and plan clearly.
shortcut: Annual raise = current salary × raise% ÷ 100. Monthly bump = ÷ 12. After-tax estimate: multiply by 0.70. Quick mental math: 5% on any salary is half of 10% — and 10% is just move the decimal.
example:
Salary: $60,000
5% raise = $3,000/year
Per month = $250
After tax ≈ $175/month

title: Overtime pay — time and a half
concept: Overtime in the US is 1.5× your regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 per week. Those extra hours pay significantly more — 8 hours of overtime at $20/hr earns you $240, not $160.
shortcut: Overtime rate = regular rate × 1.5. Multiply by overtime hours for your extra pay. At $20/hr: overtime rate = $30. 8 hours × $30 = $240 extra. Calculate before committing to a long week — overtime adds up fast.
example:
Regular rate: $20/hr
Overtime rate: $20 × 1.5 = $30/hr
8 OT hours × $30 = $240
Vs. 8 regular hours = $160

title: Compare pay across periods
concept: Job offers quote pay in different periods — weekly, bi-weekly, monthly, annual. Bi-weekly (every two weeks) is 26 pay periods per year, not 24. Converting to annual first puts every offer on the same footing.
shortcut: Annual ÷ 52 = weekly. Annual ÷ 26 = bi-weekly. Annual ÷ 12 = monthly. In reverse: bi-weekly × 26 = annual. The most common mistake: treating bi-weekly as semi-monthly (24 periods instead of 26) — it under-counts two paychecks a year.

title: Simple interest — the baseline
concept: Simple interest is the most transparent form of interest: you earn the same amount each period on the original principal. No compounding, no surprises. It's used in short-term loans, bonds, and savings accounts as a reference point.
shortcut: Interest = Principal × Rate × Time. $1,000 at 5%/year for 3 years = $1,000 × 0.05 × 3 = $150 total interest. Total balance = $1,150. The formula never changes — just substitute your numbers.
example:
Principal: $1,000
Rate: 5%/year
Time: 3 years
Interest = $1,000 × 5% × 3 = $150
Balance = $1,150

title: The Rule of 72 — when does it double?
concept: The Rule of 72 is a mental math shortcut: divide 72 by the annual interest rate to estimate how many years it takes for money to double. It works for any growth rate — investment returns, debt interest, even inflation.
shortcut: Years to double = 72 ÷ annual rate. At 8%: 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years. At 6%: 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years. At 12%: 72 ÷ 12 = 6 years. Works equally well in reverse: if something doubles in 10 years, the implied rate is ~7.2%.
example:
Savings at 4%/year:
72 ÷ 4 = 18 years to double

Debt at 12%/year:
72 ÷ 12 = 6 years to double
(if you only pay minimums)

title: Return on investment — the one number
concept: ROI (Return on Investment) puts every investment on the same scale: what percentage did you gain relative to what you put in? A $200 gain on a $1,000 investment is 20% ROI — regardless of how long it took.
shortcut: ROI% = (gain ÷ cost) × 100. Gain $50 on a $500 investment → $50 ÷ $500 × 100 = 10% ROI. To find the dollar gain from an ROI%: cost × ROI% ÷ 100. Use ROI to compare any two investments directly.

title: Round to estimate fast
concept: When you don't need an exact total, rounding each price to the nearest $10 is faster than adding exact amounts. Round first, then add the round numbers — you'll land within a few dollars every time.
shortcut: Anything ending in 1–4 rounds down. Anything 5–9 rounds up. $13 → $10, $17 → $20, $23 → $20, $28 → $30. Add the rounded numbers in your head — two or three items takes under five seconds.
example:
Items: $13 and $27
Round: $10 + $30 = $40
Actual: $40.00 ✓

Items: $17 and $22
Round: $20 + $20 = $40
Actual: $39.00 (close!)

title: Convert salary to hourly fast
concept: Whether you're comparing job offers or checking a freelance rate, the quickest salary reality check is to divide the annual figure by 2,000 — that's 40 hours × 50 working weeks, the real year.
shortcut: Annual ÷ 2,000 = hourly. Drop three zeros and halve it: $60k → $60 → $30/hr. In reverse: hourly × 2,000 = annual. $25/hr × 2,000 = $50,000/year. One step, no calculator.

title: Spot a % change instantly
concept: When a price rises or drops, find the percentage change with one move: change amount ÷ original price × 100. If a $50 item now costs $60, the change is $10 and $10 ÷ $50 = 20% — it went up 20%.
shortcut: % change = (change ÷ original) × 100. The shortcut: recognize the fraction first. Change is a quarter of the original → 25%. A fifth → 20%. A tenth → 10%. Identify the fraction, convert to a percent.

title: Double and half in a second
concept: Doubling and halving are the fastest mental operations you have. They're the foundation of 200% increases, 50% off deals, splitting bills, and finding midpoints. Speed up by splitting numbers into round parts.
shortcut: To double $37: split into $30 + $7, double each ($60 + $14), add for $74. To halve: even numbers are instant. Odd: subtract 1, halve, add $0.50. $37 ÷ 2 = $18.50.

title: Multiply by 5 the fast way
concept: Multiplying by 5 looks hard but it's just ×10 then ÷2. Since finding 10% is automatic (move the decimal), you already know the hard part. One extra halving step and you're done.
shortcut: $46 × 5: move decimal → $460, halve → $230. Works for any number. In reverse: ÷5 means ÷10 then ×2. Useful for per-item pricing, hourly rates, and 5-pack deals.
